text: Given an integer array of size n, find all elements that appear more than n over three times, rounded down. Follow-up: can you do it in linear time and constant space?

Thanks. Before I dive in, one quick observation to anchor on. How many such elements can there even be? If three distinct values each appeared more than n over three times, that's more than n elements in total — impossible. So at most two elements qualify.
Exactly. That bound is the key.
Just to confirm the output — I return the values themselves, in any order, and the answer can be empty, one, or two elements? And the threshold is strictly greater than n over three, rounded down?

Let me think about the space constraint. A naive approach would count everything in a hash map — linear time, but linear space too, so it fails the follow-up. Sorting costs n log n. This problem reminds me of Boyer-Moore majority voting, extended to two candidates. The classic vote finds a value that fills more than half the array with one candidate slot. Since at most two elements can clear a third, I keep two candidate-and-count slots instead of one.

Here's the plan, in two phases. One: keep two candidate slots, each with a count. Two: for each number, if it matches a candidate, bump that count; else if a slot is empty, adopt the number there; otherwise it's a third distinct value, so decrement both counts. Three: in a second pass, count the two candidates for real, and keep each one that appears more than n over three times. One thing worth flagging — and this is the big difference from the more-than-half version — voting alone isn't enough. A candidate can survive the vote without truly qualifying, so I must verify with a real count. In the more-than-half version a majority is guaranteed to exist; here it isn't. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The first loop is the vote, with four integers: two candidates and their counts. The second loop resets the counts and recounts the two candidates, and I push each one whose count beats the size over three. One thing worth flagging — the two match checks must come before the two empty-slot checks. If an empty slot were checked first, a number already held in the other slot could be adopted again, and the same value would sit in both slots, wasting one.

Let's dry-run the code on an input designed to trip up a missing verify. Three, three, four, two, four, four, two, four — n is eight, so the threshold is two, and the expected answer is just four. The vote ends with candidates three and four. The step that matters is the verify: three appears only twice, which is not more than two, so it's dropped. Four appears four times, so it's kept. Without the verify pass, I'd have wrongly returned three too. That matches. Corner cases: a single one returns one. One, two returns both, since each count beats zero. One, two, three returns empty — nobody beats one, and the verify catches it.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — two passes. Space is constant — just four integers, independent of n. That satisfies the follow-up. Oh, one more thing — this generalizes. For more than n over k, I'd keep k minus one candidate slots and decrement all of them on each new distinct value — n times k time, and k space. The more-than-half version is just k equals two, with one slot.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You derived the at-most-two bound before anything else. You explained why the verify pass is mandatory here, but not when a majority is guaranteed. And you generalized cleanly to the n over k version. Good work.
